prompts.evidence: Idea 1 (habit makes a thing look right, so new ideas raise an outcry for custom): d03-p003, 'a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong, gives it a superficial appearance of being right, and raises at first a formidable outcry in defense of custom'. Idea 2 (the outcry does not last): d03-p003, 'But the tumult soon subsides. Time makes more converts than reason.' The prompt names neither habit nor time.

Idea 1 (cause of all mankind, universal not local): d03-p006, 'The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind. Many circumstances ... are not local, but universal'. Idea 2 (fire and sword and war on natural rights concern everyone who can feel): d03-p006, 'The laying a country desolate with fire and sword, declaring war against the natural rights of all mankind ... is the concern of every man to whom nature hath given the power of feeling'.

Idea 1 (society from wants, government from wickedness; positive versus negative): d03-p012, 'Society is produced by our wants, and government by our wickedness; the former promotes our happiness positively by uniting our affections, the latter negatively by restraining our vices'. Idea 2 (society a blessing, government at best a necessary evil): d03-p013, 'Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil'. Idea 3 (conscience not obeyed, so part of property is given up to protect the rest, the lesser of two evils): d03-p013, 'were the impulses of conscience clear, uniform, and irresistibly obeyed, man would need no other lawgiver; but that not being the case, he finds it necessary to surrender up a part of his property to furnish means for the protection of the rest ... out of two evils to choose the least'.

Idea 1 (necessity draws them into society because one man cannot meet his wants, build alone, or survive illness or misfortune): d03-p014, 'the strength of one man is so unequal to his wants', 'one man might labour out of the common period of life without accomplishing anything', 'Disease, nay even misfortune would be death'; d03-p015, 'necessity, like a gravitating power, would soon form our newly arrived emigrants into society'. Idea 2 (once first difficulties are overcome they relax in duty, and that defect of moral virtue makes government necessary): d03-p015, 'in proportion as they surmount the first difficulties of emigration ... they will begin to relax in their duty and attachment to each other; and this remissness, will point out the necessity of establishing some form of government to supply the defect of moral virtue'.

Idea 1 (too large for all to meet, so lawmaking goes to chosen representatives): d03-p017, 'too inconvenient for all of them to meet on every occasion ... leave the legislative part to be managed by a select number chosen from the whole body'. Idea 2 (further growth: divide into parts each sending its number): d03-p017, 'divide the whole into convenient parts, each part sending its proper number'. Idea 3 (frequent elections so the elected return among the electors, share a common interest and form no separate interest): d03-p017, 'that the elected might never form to themselves an interest separate from the electors, prudence will point out the propriety of having elections often; because as the elected might by that means return and mix again with the general body of the electors', and 'this frequent interchange will establish a common interest'.

Idea 1 (the simpler a thing, the less liable to disorder and the easier repaired): d03-p019, 'the more simple anything is, the less liable it is to be disordered; and the easier repaired when disordered'. Idea 2 (the English constitution is so complex that the fault cannot be located for years): d03-p020, 'so exceedingly complex, that the nation may suffer for years together without being able to discover in which part the fault lies'. Idea 3 (under simple absolute government the people know the source and the remedy): d03-p020, 'if the people suffer, they know the head from which their suffering springs; know likewise the remedy'.

Idea 1 (remains of two ancient tyrannies plus new republican materials): d03-p021, 'the base remains of two ancient tyrannies, compounded with some new republican materials'. Idea 2 (monarchical in the King, aristocratical in the Peers, republican in the Commons): d03-p022, 'monarchical tyranny in the person of the King'; d03-p023, 'aristocratical tyranny in the persons of the Peers'; d03-p024, 'new republican materials, in the persons of the Commons'. Idea 3 (King and Peers add nothing to freedom because hereditary and independent of the people): d03-p025, 'The two first, by being hereditary, are independent of the people; wherefore in a constitutional sense they contribute nothing towards the freedom of the state'.

Idea 1 (the Commons' check presupposes the King cannot be trusted and the Commons are wiser): d03-p028, 'That the King is not to be trusted without being looked after'; d03-p029, 'That the Commons ... are either wiser or more worthy of confidence than the crown'. Idea 2 (the same constitution lets the King reject their bills, supposing him wiser than those already supposed wiser than him): d03-p030, 'gives afterwards the King a power to check the Commons, by empowering him to reject their other bills; it again supposes that the King is wiser than those whom it has already supposed to be wiser than him. A mere absurdity!'. Idea 3 (the assumptions contradict): d03-p026, 'either the words have no meaning, or they are flat contradictions'. The prompt states only that he calls it absurd, not why.

Idea 1 (the crown is the overbearing part): d03-p034, 'That the crown is this overbearing part in the English constitution needs not be mentioned'. Idea 2 (machine image: the greatest weight has its way though others slow it): d03-p033, 'as the greater weight will always carry up the less ... though the others ... may clog ... the first moving power will at last have its way'. Idea 3 (its weight comes from giving places and pensions; door locked but key given to the crown): d03-p034, 'derives its whole consequence merely from being the giver of places and pensions', 'wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy ... foolish enough to put the Crown in possession of the key'.

Idea 1 (the distinction into kings and subjects has no natural or religious reason): d03-p040, 'another and greater distinction for which no truly natural or religious reason can be assigned, and that is, the distinction of men into Kings and Subjects'. Idea 2 (male and female of nature, good and bad of heaven): d03-p040, 'Male and female are the distinctions of nature, good and bad the distinctions of heaven'. Idea 3 (rich and poor explicable without oppression): d03-p039, 'the distinctions of rich and poor may in a great measure be accounted for, and that without having recourse to the harsh ill sounding names of oppression and avarice'. Idea 4 (a race exalted like a new species): d03-p040, 'so exalted above the rest, and distinguished like some new species'.

Idea 1 (no kings, no wars; the pride of kings causes confusion): d03-p041, 'there were no kings; the consequence of which was there were no wars; it is the pride of kings which throw mankind into confusion'. Idea 2 (Holland): d03-p041, 'Holland without a king hath enjoyed more peace for this last century than any of the monarchial governments in Europe'. Idea 3 (introduced by the heathens, copied by Israel, serving idolatry; divine honours to dead kings): d03-p042, 'first introduced into the world by the Heathens, from whom the children of Israel copied the custom ... for the promotion of idolatry. The Heathens paid divine honors to their deceased kings'.

Idea 1 (Gideon, offered a hereditary crown after victory, refuses and denies their right to give it): d03-p046, 'The Jews elate with success ... proposed making him a king, saying, Rule thou over us, thou and thy son and thy son's son', 'The Lord shall rule over you', 'Gideon doth not decline the honor, but denieth their right to give it'. Idea 2 (the people ask Samuel for a king to be like other nations; God says they rejected him): d03-p047, 'make us a king to judge us like all other nations', 'they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me'. Idea 3 (Samuel's warning: sons, daughters, best fields): d03-p047, 'he will take your sons', 'he will take your daughters', 'he will take your fields and your olive yards, even the best of them'. Idea 4 (thunder and rain; the people confess the sin): d03-p047, 'the Lord sent thunder and rain that day', 'we have added unto our sins this evil, to ask a king'.

Idea 1 (men originally equal, so none may set his family above others forever; descendants may be unworthy): d03-p048, 'all men being originally equals, no one by birth could have a right to set up his own family in perpetual preference to all others forever ... his descendants might be far too unworthy to inherit them'. Idea 2 (the givers of honours could not give away posterity's right): d03-p049, 'the givers of those honors could have no power to give away the right of posterity'. Idea 3 (such a compact might put them under a rogue or a fool): d03-p049, 'might (perhaps) in the next succession put them under the government of a rogue or a fool'.

Idea 1 (the first king probably the chief ruffian of a plundering gang who made the quiet pay for safety): d03-p050, 'nothing better than the principal ruffian of some restless gang ... overawed the quiet and defenceless to purchase their safety by frequent contributions'. Idea 2 (his electors did not intend hereditary right): d03-p050, 'his electors could have no idea of giving hereditary right to his descendants'. Idea 3 (superstitious tales and fear of disorder at the choice of a new leader): d03-p050, 'to trump up some superstitious tale', 'the disorders which threatened ... on the decease of a leader and the choice of a new one'. Idea 4 (convenience later claimed as right): d03-p050, 'what at first was submitted to as a convenience, was afterwards claimed as a right'.

Idea 1 (lot, election or usurpation): d03-p052, 'either by lot, by election, or by usurpation'. Idea 2 (lot and election set a precedent that excludes inheritance): d03-p052, 'If the first king was taken by lot, it establishes a precedent for the next, which excludes hereditary succession', 'by election, that likewise establishes a precedent for the next'. Idea 3 (binding all future generations has no parallel but original sin): d03-p052, 'hath no parrallel in or out of scripture but the doctrine of original sin'. Idea 4 (usurpation nobody will defend): d03-p053, 'As to usurpation, no man will be so hardy as to defend it'.

Idea 1 (those born to reign grow insolent, live in a different world, and are often the most ignorant and unfit): d03-p054, 'Men who look upon themselves born to reign ... soon grow insolent', 'the world they act in differs so materially from the world at large', 'frequently the most ignorant and unfit of any throughout the dominions'. Idea 2 (throne held by a minor or by a king worn out with age; the public a prey to regency and miscreants): d03-p055, 'the throne is subject to be possessed by a minor at any age; all which time the regency ... have every opportunity and inducement to betray their trust', 'a king worn out with age and infirmity', 'the public becomes a prey to every miscreant'.

Idea 1 (the plea that it preserves a nation from civil wars): d03-p056, 'The most plausible plea ... is, that it preserves a nation from civil wars'. Idea 2 (false; English history since the conquest shows many civil wars and rebellions): d03-p056, 'the most barefaced falsity', 'no less than eight civil wars and nineteen rebellions'. Idea 3 (York and Lancaster): d03-p057, 'The contest ... between the houses of York and Lancaster, laid England in a scene of blood for many years'. Idea 4 (it makes against peace): d03-p056, 'instead of making for peace, it makes against it'.

Idea 1 (a king makes war and gives away places, impoverishing and dividing the nation, and is highly paid): d03-p062, 'little more to do than to make war and give away places; which, in plain terms, is to impoverish the nation and set it together by the ears', 'eight hundred thousand sterling a year'. Idea 2 (the crown's corrupt influence through places has swallowed the power and virtue of the Commons, the republican part): d03-p061, 'the corrupt influence of the crown, by having all the places in its disposal, hath so effectually swallowed up the power, and eaten out the virtue of the House of Commons (the republican part in the constitution)'. The prompt states the conclusion about France but not the reason asked for.

Idea 1 (the contest has gone from argument to arms; the King chose it and the continent accepted): d03-p065, 'Arms, as the last resource, decide the contest; the appeal was the choice of the King, and the continent hath accepted the challenge'; d03-p068, 'By referring the matter from argument to arms, a new era for politics is struck; a new method of thinking hath arisen'. Idea 2 (earlier plans all aimed at union and differed only on force or friendship): d03-p068, 'terminated in one and the same point, viz. a union with Great Britain; ... the one proposing force, the other friendship'. Idea 3 (like last year's almanacs): d03-p068, 'like the almanacs of the last year; which, though proper then, are superseded and useless now'.

Idea 1 (a continent and posterity, not a city or an age): d03-p067, 'not the affair of a city, a country, a province, or a kingdom, but of a continent', 'not the concern of a day, a year, or an age; posterity are virtually involved'. Idea 2 (seed time of union; a small fracture grows like a name cut in a young oak): d03-p067, 'Now is the seed time of continental union', 'The least fracture now will be like a name engraved with the point of a pin on the tender rind of a young oak; the wound will enlarge with the tree'.

Idea 1 (the argument is fallacious, like milk and meat): d03-p070, 'Nothing can be more fallacious than this kind of argument. We may as well assert that because a child has thrived upon milk, that it is never to have meat'. Idea 2 (America would have flourished as much or more without any European power): d03-p070, 'America would have flourished as much, and probably much more, had no European power had anything to do with her'. Idea 3 (its commerce is in necessaries that will always sell): d03-p070, 'are the necessaries of life, and will always have a market while eating is the custom of Europe'.

Idea 1 (protection from interest, trade and dominion, not attachment, and at America's expense): d03-p071, 'defended the continent at our expense as well as her own ... the sake of trade and dominion'; d03-p072, 'her motive was interest not attachment'. Idea 2 (she defended against her own enemies, who had no quarrel with Americans except as British subjects): d03-p072, 'not ... from our enemies on our account, but from her enemies on her own account, from those who had no quarrel with us on any other account'; d03-p073, 'France and Spain never were ... our enemies as Americans, but as our being the subjects of Great Britain'. Idea 3 (without the connection, peace with France and Spain): d03-p072, 'we should be at peace with France and Spain were they at war with Britain'.

Idea 1 (if true it shames Britain; brutes do not devour their young): d03-p074, 'Then the more shame upon her conduct. Even brutes do not devour their young'. Idea 2 (Europe, not England, is the parent; America an asylum for the persecuted from all Europe): d03-p074, 'Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America. This new world hath been the asylum for the persecuted lovers of civil and religious liberty from every part of Europe'. Idea 3 (less than a third of the province of English descent): d03-p076, 'Not one third of the inhabitants, even of this province, are of English descent'. Idea 4 (the widening circle: neighbour, townsman, countryman, so all Europeans in America are countrymen): d03-p076, 'all Europeans meeting in America, or any other quarter of the globe, are countrymen'.

Idea 1 (the connection involves America in European wars and sets it against nations that would seek its friendship): d03-p081, 'tends directly to involve this continent in European wars and quarrels; and sets us at variance with nations, who would otherwise seek our friendship'. Idea 2 (trade ruined whenever Britain is at war): d03-p082, 'whenever a war breaks out between England and any foreign power, the trade of America goes to ruin, because of her connection with Britain'. Idea 3 (commerce and a free port secure the peace and friendship of Europe; neutrality): d03-p079, 'Our plan is commerce, and that, well attended to, will secure us the peace and friendship of all Europe; because, it is the interest of all Europe to have America a free port'; d03-p082, 'neutrality in that case would be a safer convoy than a man of war'.

Idea 1 (distance): d03-p082, 'Even the distance at which the Almighty hath placed England and America is a strong and natural proof'. Idea 2 (time of discovery, before the Reformation, as a sanctuary): d03-p082, 'The reformation was preceded by the discovery of America, as if the Almighty graciously meant to open a sanctuary to the persecuted'. Idea 3 (manner of peopling): d03-p082, 'the manner in which it was peopled increases the force of it'. Idea 4 (British authority must end and so secures nothing for posterity): d03-p083, 'a form of government, which sooner or later must have an end', 'not sufficiently lasting to ensure anything which we may bequeath to posterity'.

Idea 1 (four kinds): d03-p085, 'Interested men, who are not to be trusted; weak men, who cannot see; prejudiced men, who will not see; and a certain set of moderate men, who think better of the European world than it deserves'. Idea 2 (the moderate men do the most harm): d03-p085, 'this last class, by an ill-judged deliberation, will be the cause of more calamities to this continent, than all the other three'.

Idea 1 (the test of natural feeling: can you love, honour and serve the power that brought fire and sword): d03-p087, 'bring the doctrine of reconciliation to the touchstone of nature, and then tell me, whether you can hereafter love, honour, and faithfully serve the power that hath carried fire and sword into your land'. Idea 2 (a forced connection will relapse into worse): d03-p087, 'will be forced and unnatural ... will in a little time fall into a relapse more wretched than the first'. Idea 3 (one who has suffered and still shakes hands with the murderers has a coward's heart): d03-p087, 'still can shake hands with the murderers ... you have the heart of a coward'.

Idea 1 (quiet methods failed; petitions rejected and feed kings' vanity and obstinacy): d03-p090, 'Every quiet method for peace hath been ineffectual. Our prayers have been rejected with disdain ... nothing flatters vanity or confirms obstinacy in Kings more than repeated petitioning'. Idea 2 (reconciliation a fallacious dream; nature deserted the connection; no plan short of separation gives a year's security): d03-p089, 'cannot ... compass a plan short of separation, which can promise the continent even a year's security. Reconciliation is now a fallacious dream. Nature hath deserted the connection'. Idea 3 (final separation, not leaving it to the next generation): d03-p090, 'let us come to a final separation, and not leave the next generation to be cutting throats'.

Idea 1 (too distant and too ignorant of America to manage its weighty, intricate business): d03-p092, 'the business of it will soon be too weighty, and intricate, to be managed ... by a power so distant from us, and so very ignorant of us'. Idea 2 (thousands of miles with a petition and months for an answer will look like folly): d03-p092, 'To be always running three or four thousand miles with a tale or a petition, waiting four or five months for an answer ... will in a few years be looked upon as folly and childishness'. Idea 3 (absurd for an island to govern a continent; satellite and planet; England to Europe, America to itself): d03-p093, 'something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island. In no instance hath nature made the satellite larger than its primary planet ... England to Europe, America to itself'.

Idea 1 (the object must bear a just proportion to the expense): d03-p096, 'The object, contended for, ought always to bear some just proportion to the expense'. Idea 2 (with the continent in arms and millions spent, repeal or removal of a ministry is too small): d03-p096, 'The removal of North, or the whole detestable junto, is a matter unworthy the millions we have expended', 'if the whole continent must take up arms ... it is scarcely worth our while to fight against a contemptible ministry only'. Idea 3 (independence must come sooner or later, so fighting was worthwhile only in earnest): d03-p096, 'an event which sooner or later must arrive', 'it was not worth the while to have disputed a matter, which time would have finally redressed, unless we meant to be in earnest'.

Idea 1 (the King, an enemy to liberty and jealous of American prosperity, keeps a negative over all legislation, allows only laws that suit him and keeps the continent low): d03-p098, 'he will have a negative over the whole legislation of this continent', 'such an inveterate enemy to liberty', 'he will suffer no law to be made here, but such as suit his purpose', 'to keep this continent as low and humble as possible', 'the power who is jealous of our prosperity'. Idea 2 (the negative is more dangerous in America than in England, because of defence bills and his residence): d03-p099, 'England being the King's residence, and America not so', 'ten times more dangerous and fatal ... there he will scarcely refuse his consent to a bill for putting England into as strong a state of defence as possible, and in America he would never suffer such a bill to be passed'. Idea 3 (he might repeal the acts to gain by craft what force cannot): d03-p100, 'it would be policy in the king at this time, to repeal the acts ... that he may accomplish by craft and subtlety, in the long run, what he cannot do by force'.

Idea 1 (the best terms are only a temporary expedient, a guardianship until the colonies come of age): d03-p101, 'no more than a temporary expedient, or a kind of government by guardianship, which can last no longer than till the colonies come of age'. Idea 2 (government hangs by a thread; emigrants of property stay away and inhabitants sell up and leave): d03-p101, 'Emigrants of property will not choose to come to a country whose form of government hangs but by a thread ... numbers of the present inhabitants would lay hold of the interval, to dispense of their effects, and quit the continent'.

Idea 1 (reconciliation is the likelier cause of revolt): d03-p102, 'it is more than probable, that it will be followed by a revolt somewhere or other'; d03-p103, 'ten times more to dread from a patched up connection than from independance'. Idea 2 (the ruined will not submit; Britain's power only on paper): d03-p103, 'having nothing more to lose, they disdain submission', 'whose power will be wholly on paper'. Idea 3 (the colonies have shown good order): d03-p104, 'such a spirit of good order and obedience to continental government'. Idea 4 (no distinctions, no temptation; republics at peace, monarchies never long at rest): d03-p105, 'Where there are no distinctions there can be no superiority, perfect equality affords no temptation. The republics of Europe are all ... in peace', 'Monarchical governments ... are never long at rest'.

Idea 1 (annual assemblies with a president only, domestic business, under a Continental Congress): d03-p107, 'Let the assemblies be annual, with a President only ... their business wholly domestic, and subject to the authority of a Continental Congress'. Idea 2 (colonies divided into districts sending delegates): d03-p108, 'Let each colony be divided into six, eight, or ten, convenient districts, each district to send a proper number of delegates to Congress'. Idea 3 (president chosen from a colony taken by lot, in rotation): d03-p108, 'let a colony be taken from the whole thirteen colonies by lot ... a president from out of the delegates of that province ... till the whole thirteen shall have had their proper rotation'. Idea 4 (three fifths for a law): d03-p108, 'not less than three fifths of the Congress to be called a majority'.

Idea 1 (a Continental Conference, an intermediate body between Congress and the people): d03-p109, 'some intermediate body between the governed and the governors, that is, between the Congress and the people, let a Continental Conference be held'. Idea 2 (its composition; knowledge and power united): d03-p110, 'A committee of twenty-six members of Congress ... Two members from each House of Assembly, or Provincial Convention; and five representatives of the people at large', 'will be united, the two grand principles of business, knowledge and power'. Idea 3 (the charter fixes how members are chosen and their jurisdiction, secures freedom, property and above all religion; then the Conference dissolves): d03-p111, 'fixing the number and manner of choosing members of Congress, members of Assembly ... drawing the line of business and jurisdiction between them', 'Securing freedom and property to all men, and above all things, the free exercise of religion', 'Immediately after which, the said Conference to dissolve'.

Idea 1 (he reigns above): d03-p113, 'I'll tell you, friend, he reigns above'. Idea 2 (a day to proclaim the charter, placed on the word of God with a crown on it, to show that the law is king): d03-p113, 'let a day be solemnly set apart for proclaiming the charter; let it be brought forth placed on the divine law, the word of God; let a crown be placed thereon, by which the world may know ... that in America the law is king'. Idea 3 (the crown then demolished and scattered among the people): d03-p113, 'let the crown at the conclusion of the ceremony be demolished, and scattered among the people whose right it is'.

Idea 1 (natural right; wiser and safer to form a constitution coolly while they can): d03-p114, 'A government of our own is our natural right ... infinitely wiser and safer, to form a constitution of our own in a cool deliberate manner, while we have it in our power'. Idea 2 (otherwise someone may gather the desperate and discontented, seize government and sweep away liberties): d03-p114, 'laying hold of popular disquietudes, may collect together the desperate and the discontented, and by assuming to themselves the powers of government, may sweep away the liberties of the continent like a deluge'. Idea 3 (under restored British rule the tottering state would tempt an adventurer and Britain could not help in time): d03-p114, 'the tottering situation of things will be a temptation for some desperate adventurer ... what relief can Britain give? Ere she could hear the news, the fatal business might be done'. The answer does not use the footnote on Massanello.

Idea 1 (injuries nature cannot forgive): d03-p116, 'There are injuries which nature cannot forgive'. Idea 2 (reason forbids faith; kinship wears out daily while quarrels multiply): d03-p115, 'those in whom our reason forbids us to have faith', 'Every day wears out the little remains of kindred between us and them', 'ten times more and greater concerns to quarrel over'. Idea 3 (lover and ravisher): d03-p116, 'As well can the lover forgive the ravisher of his mistress, as the continent forgive the murders of Britain'. Idea 4 (the feelings were implanted for good purposes; without them the guilty escape and justice vanishes): d03-p116, 'implanted in us these unextinguishable feelings for good and wise purposes', 'justice be extirpated the earth', 'The robber and the murderer would often escape unpunished'.

Idea 1 (strength in unity not numbers, yet numbers sufficient): d03-p121, 'It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies; yet our present numbers are sufficient to repel the force of all the world'. Idea 2 (largest armed and disciplined body; no single colony can support itself but the whole united can): d03-p121, 'the largest body of armed and disciplined men of any power under Heaven', 'no single colony is able to support itself, and the whole, when united, can accomplish the matter'. Idea 3 (not crowded: fewer seaports to defend and lose; numbers proportioned to wants so none need be idle): d03-p122, 'The more sea port towns we had, the more should we have both to defend and to lose. Our present numbers are so happily proportioned to our wants, that no man need be idle'.

Idea 1 (a settled independent government is cheap at any price; millions spent only for repeal leave posterity the work and a debt): d03-p123, 'Can we but leave posterity with a settled form of government, an independant constitution of its own, the purchase at any price will be cheap. But to expend millions for the sake of getting a few vile acts repealed ... leaving them the great work to do, and a debt upon their backs'. Idea 2 (a national debt is a national bond, no grievance without interest): d03-p124, 'A national debt is a national bond; and when it bears no interest, is in no case a grievance'. Idea 3 (Britain's debt is compensated by a navy; for a twentieth of it America could have one as large again): d03-p124, 'as a compensation for her debt, she has a large navy ... for the twentieth part of the English national debt, could have a navy as large again'. Nothing in the answer depends on the tables d03-p127 or d03-p129.

Idea 1 (America produces the materials and needs nothing from abroad): d03-p130, 'Tar, timber, iron, and cordage are her natural produce. We need go abroad for nothing'. Idea 2 (natural manufactory and greatest pride): d03-p130, 'it being the natural manufactory of this country'; d03-p131, 'Shipbuilding is America's greatest pride'. Idea 3 (an article of commerce uniting commerce and protection, worth more than it cost, saleable for gold and silver): d03-p130, 'view the building a fleet as an article of commerce', 'A navy when finished is worth more than it cost', 'commerce and protection are united', 'if we want them not, we can sell; and by that means replace our paper currency with ready gold and silver'.

Idea 1 (the power that tried to subdue is the most improper to defend; conquest under pretence of friendship): d03-p133, 'the power which hath endeavoured to subdue us, is of all others, the most improper to defend us. Conquest may be effected under the pretence of friendship'. Idea 2 (if her ships are not in American harbours, a navy thousands of miles off is of little use): d03-p133, 'if her ships are not to be admitted into our harbours ... A navy three or four thousand miles off can be of little use, and on sudden emergencies, none at all'. Idea 3 (protect ourselves for ourselves): d03-p133, 'if we must hereafter protect ourselves, why not do it for ourselves? Why do it for another?'.

Idea 1 (few listed ships are fit for service and they are spread over many stations): d03-p134, 'not a tenth part of them are at any one time fit for service', 'not a fifth part of such as are fit for service, can be spared on any one station', 'The East and West Indies, Mediterranean, Africa ... make large demands upon her navy'. Idea 2 (no foreign dominion, so the whole force on its own coast with two to one advantage over ships sailing thousands of miles): d03-p134, 'as we neither have, nor claim any foreign dominion, our whole force would be employed on our own coast, where we should ... have two to one the advantage of those who had three or four thousand miles to sail over ... and the same distance to return in order to refit'. Idea 3 (West Indies trade at America's mercy): d03-p134, 'her trade to the West Indies, which ... is entirely at its mercy'.

Idea 1 (population and trade absorb men and lower patriotic and military spirit; those with more to lose venture less): d03-p138, 'trade being the consequence of population, men become too much absorbed thereby', 'Commerce diminishes the spirit, both of patriotism and military defence', 'The more men have to lose, the less willing are they to venture'. Idea 2 (variety of interests would make union hard later): d03-p139, 'It might be difficult, if not impossible, to form the Continent into one government half a century hence. The vast variety of interests ... would create confusion'. Idea 3 (young and tried by distress, so now is the time): d03-p139, 'the friendship which is formed in misfortune, are, of all others, the most lasting', 'we are young, and we have been distressed; but our concord hath withstood our troubles', 'the present time is the true time for establishing it'.

Idea 1 (the once-only time of forming itself into a government): d03-p140, 'that peculiar time, which never happens to a nation but once, viz. the time of forming itself into a government'. Idea 2 (most nations let it slip, took laws from conquerors, had a king first): d03-p140, 'Most nations have let slip the opportunity, and ... have been compelled to receive laws from their conquerors', 'First, they had a king, and then a form of government'. Idea 3 (charter first, men delegated afterwards): d03-p140, 'the articles or charter of government, should be formed first, and men delegated to execute them afterward'. Idea 4 (else a fortunate ruffian, as with William the Conqueror): d03-p141, 'When William the Conqueror subdued England, he gave them law at the point of the sword ... we shall be in danger of having it filled by some fortunate ruffian, who may treat us in the same manner'.

Idea 1 (government's only business with religion is to protect its conscientious professors): d03-p142, 'the indispensable duty of all government, to protect all conscientious professors thereof, and I know of no other business which government hath to do therewith'. Idea 2 (diversity is the will of the Almighty, a larger field for Christian kindness): d03-p142, 'it is the will of the Almighty, that there should be diversity of religious opinions among us: It affords a larger field for our Christian kindness'. Idea 3 (denominations as children of one family): d03-p142, 'like children of the same family, differing only, in what is called, their Christian names'.

Idea 1 (few electors or representatives dangerous, unequal ones more so; Pennsylvania's two counties): d03-p144, 'A small number of electors, or a small number of representatives, are equally dangerous. But if the number of the representatives be not only small, but unequal, the danger is increased', 'this whole province had been governed by two counties only'. Idea 2 (choosing through the assemblies was proper in necessity, but expedience and right differ): d03-p145, 'Expedience and right are different things', 'no method so ready, or at that time so proper, as to appoint persons from the several Houses of Assembly'. Idea 3 (his question about one body holding representation and election): d03-p145, 'whether representation and election is not too great a power for one and the same body of men to possess?'.

Idea 1 (no power can mediate while America calls itself a subject): d03-p148, 'while America calls herself the Subject of Great Britain, no power ... can offer her mediation'. Idea 2 (France and Spain will not help merely to repair the connection): d03-p149, 'unreasonable to suppose, that France or Spain will give us any kind of assistance, if we mean only ... repairing the breach'. Idea 3 (considered rebels by foreign nations): d03-p150, 'we must, in the eye of foreign nations, be considered as rebels'. Idea 4 (a manifesto to foreign courts would do more good than petitions): d03-p151, 'such a memorial would produce more good effects to this Continent, than if a ship were freighted with petitions to Britain'. Idea 5 (only by independence can they be received abroad and take rank with nations): d03-p152, 'we can neither be received nor heard abroad ... until, by an independance, we take rank with other nations'.

Idea 1 (instead of terrifying it prepared the way for independence; men read by way of revenge): d03-p155, 'Men read by way of revenge. And the Speech, instead of terrifying, prepared a way for the manly principles of Independance'. Idea 2 (a wilful libel against truth, the common good and mankind): d03-p156, 'a wilful audacious libel against the truth, the common good, and the existence of mankind'. Idea 3 (its one good quality: it cannot deceive, brutality on its face): d03-p156, 'The Speech hath one good quality, which is, that it is not calculated to deceive ... Brutality and tyranny appear on the face of it'.

Idea 1 (the King has broken every obligation and earned universal hatred): d03-p158, 'he hath wickedly broken through every moral and human obligation ... procured for himself an universal hatred'. Idea 2 (America's interest is to provide for herself and her young family rather than grant away her property to such a power): d03-p158, 'It is now the interest of America to provide for herself. She hath already a large and young family, whom it is more her duty to take care of, than to be granting away her property, to support a power who is become a reproach'.

Idea 1 (no dependent nation with limited commerce and fettered legislation reaches eminence): d03-p161, 'no nation in a state of foreign dependance, limited in its commerce, and cramped and fettered in its legislative powers, can ever arrive at any material eminence'. Idea 2 (progress so far is childhood compared with what legislative power in her own hands would allow): d03-p161, 'it is but childhood, compared with what she would be capable of arriving at, had she ... the legislative powers in her own hands'. Idea 3 (England benefits by commerce not conquest, and that would largely continue): d03-p161, 'It is the commerce and not the conquest of America by which England is to be benefited, and that would in a great measure continue, were the countries as independant of each other as France and Spain'.

Idea 1 (military ability comes from the last war's experience, which would be extinct later, leaving no general or officer): d03-p164, 'our military ability, at this time, arises from the experience gained in the last war, and which in forty or fifty years time, would have been totally extinct. The Continent, would not, by that time, have had a General, or even a military officer left'. Idea 2 (experience without numbers then, numbers without experience later, so the right point lies between and is now): d03-p164, 'at the conclusion of the last war, we had experience, but wanted numbers; and forty or fifty years hence, we should have numbers, without experience ... And that point of time is the present time'.

Idea 1 (sale of the back lands sinks the debt without burden; the quit-rent in time supports government): d03-p167, 'It is by the sale of those lands that the debt may be sunk, without burden to any, and the quit-rent reserved thereon, will always lessen, and in time will wholly support the yearly expense of government'. Idea 2 (if Britain stays sovereign the means of sinking the debt are lost; the lands were taken by the unjust extension of Canada's limits): d03-p166, 'Should affairs be patched up with Britain, and she to remain the governing and sovereign power ... we shall deprive ourselves of the very means of sinking the debt', 'the back lands which some of the provinces are clandestinely deprived of, by the unjust extension of the limits of Canada'.

Idea 1 (no law or government, power only by courtesy, held together by a concurrence of sentiment that enemies try to dissolve): d03-p170, 'Without law, without government, without any other mode of power than what is founded on, and granted by courtesy. Held together by an unexampled concurrence of sentiment, which ... every secret enemy is endeavouring to dissolve'. Idea 2 (no property secure, no treason, everyone acts as he pleases): d03-p170, 'The property of no man is secure', 'there is no such thing as treason; wherefore, everyone thinks himself at liberty to act as he pleases'. Idea 3 (too loosely held; if nothing is done neither course will be practicable): d03-p171, 'The Continental Belt is too loosely buckled. And if something is not done in time ... neither Reconciliation nor Independance will be practicable'.

Idea 1 (Britain cannot and will not offer it; no means to hold a faithless court to it, a later parliament may repeal, no law between nations): d03-p173, 'the request is not now in the power of Britain to comply with, neither will she propose it', 'By what means is such a corrupt and faithless court to be kept to its engagements? Another parliament ... may hereafter repeal the obligation', 'No going to law with nations'. Idea 2 (circumstances too must be restored: towns, losses, debts): d03-p173, 'our burnt and destroyed towns repaired or built up, our private losses made good, our public debts (contracted for defence) discharged'. Idea 3 (a year ago it would have won the continent; now too late): d03-p173, 'had it been complied with a year ago, would have won the heart and soul of the Continent, but now it is too late'.

Idea 1 (not the repeal of a pecuniary law; lives too valuable for such trifles): d03-p174, 'the taking up arms, merely to enforce the repeal of a pecuniary law, seems as unwarrantable ...', 'the lives of men are too valuable to be cast away on such trifles'. Idea 2 (violence to persons, destruction of property, invasion): d03-p174, 'the violence which is done and threatened to our persons; the destruction of our property by an armed force; the invasion of our country by fire and sword, which conscientiously qualifies the use of arms'. Idea 3 (subjection should have ceased then; independence dates from the first musket): d03-p174, 'the instant, in which such a mode of defence became necessary, all subjection to Britain ought to have ceased; and the independancy of America, should have been considered, as dating its era from ... the first musket that was fired against her'.

Idea 1 (three ways): d03-p175, 'By the legal voice of the people in Congress; by a military power; or by a mob'. Idea 2 (by the first, every opportunity to form the noblest constitution and begin the world again): d03-p175, 'we have every opportunity and every encouragement before us, to form the noblest purest constitution on the face of the earth. We have it in our power to begin the world over again'. Idea 3 (soldiers may not always be citizens nor the multitude reasonable; virtue not hereditary nor perpetual): d03-p175, 'It may not always happen that our soldiers are citizens, and the multitude a body of reasonable men; virtue ... is not hereditary, neither is it perpetual'.

Idea 1 (the only bond to keep them together): d03-p177, 'Independance is the only Bond that can tye and keep us together'. Idea 2 (Britain's pride less hurt treating with states than with rebellious subjects; delay encourages hope of conquest): d03-p177, 'the pride of that court will be less hurt by treating with the American states for terms of peace, than with those, whom she denominates rebellious subjects', 'It is our delaying it that encourages her to hope for conquest'. Idea 3 (redress grievances independently, then offer to open trade; mercantile England with us; else other courts): d03-p177, 'by independantly redressing them ourselves, and then offering to open the trade. The mercantile and reasonable part in England, will be still with us ... if this offer be not accepted, other courts may be applied to'.

Idea 1 (tranquillity and confidence in his absence and indifference at his return prove a king's absence is preferable; he is a superfluity and a burden): d04-p003, 'The serene tranquillity, the mutual confidence ... during the time of the late King's escape, the indifference with which we beheld him return, are unequivocal proofs that the absence of a King is more desirable than his presence ... a political superfluity, but a grievous burden'. Idea 2 (abdication by the act of flight, not its length): d04-p005, 'He has abdicated the throne in having fled from his post. Abdication and desertion are not characterized by the length of absence; but by the single act of flight'. Idea 3 (perjured, fled in disguise toward the frontier; confidence cannot return): d04-p006, 'The nation can never give back its confidence to a man who, false to his trust, perjured to his oath, conspires a clandestine flight ... under the disguise of a valet, directs his course towards a frontier'.

Idea 1 (an office needing neither experience nor ability, left to birth, fillable by an idiot, madman or tyrant, is show not use, and may still be dangerous): d04-p010, 'requires for its execution neither experience nor ability, that may be abandoned to the desperate chance of birth, that may be filled by an idiot, a madman, a tyrant ... it is a place of show, not of use', 'may not at the same time be extremely dangerous'. Idea 2 (the thirty millions could reduce taxes, relieving the people and stopping corruption): d04-p011, 'The thirty millions which it costs to support a King ... presents us with an easy method of reducing taxes, which reduction would at once relieve the people, and stop the progress of political corruption'. Idea 3 (grandeur lies in a nation's sense of its dignity, not thrones): d04-p011, 'not ... in the splendour of thrones, but in a conspicuous sense of their own dignity'. The prompt names the two labels but not the reasons the answer supplies.

Idea 1 (brigands subdue a country and their chief takes the title of king): d05-p009, 'Bands of brigands unite to subvert a country ... the chieftain of the robbers adopts the title of monarch or king'. Idea 2 (a second brigand dispossesses him and reigns): d05-p010, 'A second brigand arrives ... he dispossesses the first; he chains him, kills him, reigns in his place'. Idea 3 (time effaces the origin; successors corrupt, invent genealogies, take religion as lifeguard; usurped power becomes hereditary right): d05-p010, 'time effaces the memory of this origin', 'they corrupt all who surround them; they invent fictitious genealogies to make their families sacred', 'they take Religion for a lifeguard: thenceforth ... the usurped power becomes an hereditary right'.

Idea 1 (one man is out of proportion to a nation's affairs): d05-p013, 'the prince is nearly always too small: where is the proportion between one man and the affairs of a whole nation?'. Idea 2 (a man of genius is driven to conquest and despotism while subjects starve praising his glory): d05-p014, 'the ambition of such a man impels him to conquest and despotism, his subjects soon have to lament his glory, and sing their Te-Deums while perishing with hunger'. Idea 3 (ordinary men and petty intriguers bring incapacity and vice): d05-p015, 'if ordinary men in power repay you with incapacity or with princely vices', 'commonplace knaves, petty intriguers'. Idea 4: d05-p015, 'monarchs do nothing, and their ministers do evil'.

Idea 1 (ancestors cannot transmit a right they did not have; no authority over the unborn; not the slave of the dead): d05-p016, 'how could they transmit to him a right they did not possess? Man has no authority over generations unborn. I cannot be the slave of the dead, more than of the living'. Idea 2 (to inherit government is to inherit peoples like herds, treating descendants as cattle without will or rights): d05-p017, 'Are we then to treat our descendants in advance as cattle, who shall have neither will nor rights of their own? To inherit government is to inherit peoples, as if they were herds'.

Idea 1 (hereditary succession makes kings what they are, as a marsh breeds vipers): d05-p018, 'it is hereditary succession that makes them what they are: this breeds monsters as a marsh breeds vipers'. Idea 2 (the prince's logic: power from birth, birth from God, so he owes nothing to men): d05-p019, 'I derive my power from my birth; I derive my birth from God; therefore I owe nothing to men'. Idea 3 (sympathy comes from putting oneself in another's place, which a monarch never can): d05-p020, 'It is by sympathy that we are good and human', 'a monarch pities none, because he has never been, can never be, in any other place than his own'. Idea 4 (the egoist above all): d05-p021, 'A monarch is an egoist by nature, the egoist par excellence'.

Idea 1 (a workman needs talent, a king only the human shape; infants or idiots may fill the office): d05-p025, 'What then is this office, which may be filled by infants or idiots? Some talent is required to be a simple workman; to be a king there is need to have only the human shape'. Idea 2 (great men seldom have worthy children; hereditary administrator as absurd as author by birthright): d05-p025, 'there can hardly be cited an instance of a great man having children worthy of him', 'an hereditary administrator is as absurd as an author by birthright'. Idea 3 (a people that bows to it is debased, paying equal homage to vice and virtue; no institution has caused more intellectual degeneracy): d05-p026, 'a people who can bow down in honor of a silly thing is a debased people', 'render equal homage to vice and virtue', 'none has caused more intellectual degeneracy'.

Idea 1 (against powerful men: rights of man, equality, a good constitution with divided powers, no privileges or monopolies, free industry, trade and press, and all will be under the law): d05-p030, 'Establish the Rights of Man; enthrone Equality; form a good Constitution; divide well its powers; let there be no privileges, no distinctions of birth, no monopolies; make safe the liberty of industry and of trade ... freedom of the press ... all citizens will be under the Law'. Idea 2 (against the legislature: representatives often renewed who neither administer nor judge, assemblies convocable at any moment, a people that can read and defend itself): d05-p032, 'With representatives, frequently renewed, who neither administer nor judge ... primary assemblies, which can be convoked any moment; with a people knowing how to read, and how to defend itself ... a Legislature would have a good deal of trouble in enjoying any months of tyranny. Let us not suppose an evil for the sake of its remedy'. The prompt states the royalist claims (d05-p029, d05-p031), not the replies.

Idea 1 (hereditary succession alone produced the civil wars of France and England; royal families' claims brought foreign wars; heredity caused the troubles of regency): d05-p036, 'hereditary succession alone has produced the civil wars of France and England', 'the pretended rights, of royal families which have twenty times drawn on these nations the scourge of foreign wars', 'the heredity of crowns that has caused the troubles of Regency'. Idea 2 (an elective chief would not be a king with courtiers, pomp, idolatry and thirty millions): d05-p037, 'that chief will not be a king surrounded by courtiers, burdened with pomp, inflated by idolatries, and endowed with thirty millions of money'.

Idea 1 (the list of rights): d06-p003, 'liberty, equality, security, property, social protection, and resistance to oppression'. Idea 2 (liberty is the right to do what is not contrary to others' rights, limited only by what secures the same rights to others): d06-p004, 'Liberty consists in the right to do whatever is not contrary to the rights of others ... no limits other than those which secure to other members of society enjoyment of the same rights'. Idea 3 (preserved by submission to the law, expression of the general will): d06-p005, 'The preservation of liberty depends on submission to the Law, which is the expression of the general will'.

Idea 1 (no accusation, arrest or detention except in cases and forms set by law; other acts arbitrary and null): d06-p013, 'None should be sued, accused, arrested, or detained, save in cases determined by the law ... Every other act against a citizen is arbitrary and null'. Idea 2 (those who carry out such acts punished; citizens may repel them by force but must obey a lawful summons): d06-p014, 'are culpable, and should be punished'; d06-p015, 'the right to repel force by force; but every citizen summoned or arrested by authority of the Law ... should instantly obey'. Idea 3 (presumption of innocence, no needless rigour): d06-p016, 'presumed innocent until legally pronounced guilty ... all rigor not necessary to secure his person should be severely repressed'. Idea 4 (law prior to the offence; retroactivity a crime): d06-p017, 'promulgated anterior to the offence'; d06-p018, 'Retroactive effect given to the law is a crime'. Idea 5 (necessary, proportioned penalties): d06-p019, 'only penalties strictly and evidently necessary ... proportioned to offences'. The answer is a full list, but each item is plain and a reader recalling the main protections can grade fairly.

Idea 1 (sovereignty one and indivisible, in the whole people, each citizen sharing equally): d06-p028, 'one, indivisible, imprescriptible, and inalienable'; d06-p029, 'It resides essentially in the whole people, and every citizen has an equal right to unite in its exercise'. Idea 2 (no group or individual may exercise authority without legal delegation): d06-p030, 'No partial assemblage of citizens, and no individual, may attribute to themselves sovereignty, or exercise any authority ... without formal delegation thereto by the law'. Idea 3 (three cases of oppression): d06-p034, 'when any law violates the natural rights, civil and political, which it should guarantee'; d06-p035, 'when the law is violated by public officials in its application to individual cases'; d06-p036, 'when arbitrary actions violate the rights of citizen against the express purpose (expression) of the law'.

Idea 1 (other arts and sciences improved, government stood still, because the old systems rest on a false principle, put antiquity for principle, forbid inquiry and use power to prevent detection): d07-p003, 'the science of government has stood still', 'their antiquity is put in the place of principle; it is forbidden to investigate their origin', 'they are established on a principle that is false, and they employ their power to prevent detection'. Idea 2 (easy to understand if begun at the right point): d07-p004, 'the least mysterious and the most easy to be understood ... if it begins its enquiries at the right point'. Idea 3 (begin with the primary divisions, not the subdivisions): d07-p005, 'Instead then of embarrassing the subject in the outset with the numerous subdivisions ... such as aristocracy, democracy, oligarchy, monarchy ... begin with what may be called primary divisions'.

Idea 1 (the two divisions): d07-p007, 'government by election and representation'; d07-p008, 'government by hereditary succession'. Idea 2 (mixed government no exception): d07-p009, 'the parts separately considered are either representative or hereditary'. Idea 3 (a negative proved on one of two amounts to an affirmative on the other): d07-p011, 'a negative proved on one thing, where two only are offered, and one must be accepted, amounts to an affirmative on the other'. Idea 4 (monarchy, royalty and aristocracy are signs of the hereditary system and fall with it): d07-p012, 'they are but secondary things or signs of the hereditary system, and which fall of themselves if that system has not a right to exist'.

Idea 1 (a right to continue depends on a right to begin): d07-p016, 'If it had not a right to begin, it has not a right to continue'. Idea 2 (no family has a superior right; the first families had no more right than Robespierre; it belongs to none): d07-p017, 'was no other than the right which Robespierre had to do the same thing in France. If he had none, they had none ... it is impossible to discover superiority of right in any family ... It belongs exclusively to none'.

Idea 1 (time has no operation on principle; an old wrong is as wrong, a new right as right): d07-p019, 'time has no more connection with, or influence upon principle ... The wrong which began a thousand years ago, is as much a wrong as if it began today; and the right which originates today, is as much a right as if it had the sanction of a thousand years'. Idea 2 (the wrong begins for us when we begin to live, and our right to resist is the same): d07-p019, 'that is the point of time at which it begins to us; and our right to resist it is the same as if it never existed before'.

Idea 1 (minors' rights are as sacred, kept under guardianship until they come of age; the guardian cannot dispossess): d07-p022, 'The rights of minors are as sacred as the rights of the aged ... to be preserved inviolate for the inheritance of the minors when they shall come of age ... the guardian cannot dispossess him'. Idea 2 (such a law subjects the minor to a system he could neither consent nor object to): d07-p022, 'to subjugate him to a system of government to which, during his minority, he could neither consent nor object'. Idea 3 (born a few years sooner he could have voted against it; so the law annuls his rights and the right to make it cannot exist): d07-p023, 'had happened to have been born a few years sooner ... to have voted against it', 'a law to take away and annul the rights of every person in the nation who shall be a minor ... consequently the right to make it cannot exist'. The prompt names the minors as the case to consider but not the reasoning.

Idea 1 (a nation is in continual renewal; no part of the flood of generations has superior authority): d07-p025, 'continually in a state of renewal and succession'; d07-p026, 'In this ever running flood of generations there is no part superior in authority to another'. Idea 2 (tenants for life in the freehold of rights, which belongs to the whole family of man): d07-p026, 'our ancestors, like ourselves, were but tenants for life in the great freehold of rights ... it belongs to the whole family of man'. Idea 3 (every generation equal in rights and as free as the one before; governing beyond the grave; no property in following generations): d07-p030, 'every generation is equal in rights to another', 'as free to act for itself in all cases, as the age and generation that preceded it. The vanity and presumption of governing beyond the grave is the most ridiculous and insolent of all tyrannies', 'neither has one generation a property in the generations that are to follow'.

Idea 1 (those above twenty-one at the time counted from, in whom legal authority resides): d07-p028, 'the persons in whom legal authority resides ... it comprehends all those who are above the age of twenty-one years, at the time that we count from'. Idea 2 (in authority fourteen to twenty-one years, until minors come of age outnumber the former stock): d07-p028, 'will continue in authority between fourteen and twenty-one years, that is, until the number of minors, who shall have arrived at age, shall be greater than the number of persons remaining of the former stock'.

Idea 1 (the first generation lives under a government of its own choice; hereditary succession follows only on its death): d07-p037, 'does not live under a hereditary government, but under a government of its own choice and establishment', 'hereditary succession can only follow on the death of the first parties'. Idea 2 (it changes from legislator to testator, taking the rights and free agency by which itself acted): d07-p039, 'It changes itself from a Legislator to a Testator ... to take from the commencing generation, and all future ones, the rights and free agency by which itself acted'. Idea 3 (precluding consent is despotism; sold by a parent is aggravation): d07-p035, 'It operates to preclude the consent of the succeeding generations; and the preclusion of consent is despotism', 'It is no relief, but an aggravation to a person in slavery, to reflect that he was sold by his parent'.

Idea 1 (rights are not devisable, transferable or annihilable, only descendable; no generation can cut off the descent): d07-p041, 'neither devisable or transferable, nor annihilable, but are descendable only, and it is not in the power of any generation to intercept finally, and cut off the descent'. Idea 2 (one generation's slavery does not lessen the next one's right to be free; wrongs have no legal descent): d07-p041, 'it does not lessen the right of the succeeding generation to be free. Wrongs cannot have a legal descent'. Idea 3 (A, B and C): d07-p042, 'A cannot make a will to take from B the property of B, and give it to C; yet this is the manner in which ... hereditary succession by law operates'.

Idea 1 (the English parliament of 1688 made William and Mary king and queen and bound the people and posterity to their heirs forever): d07-p044, 'imported a man and his wife from Holland, William and Mary, and made them king and queen of England', 'submit ourselves, our heirs, and posterities, to William and Mary, their heirs and posterities, forever'. Idea 2 (the French constituent assembly of 1789 did the same for the Capets): d07-p045, 'fell into the same vice ... an hereditary succession in the family of the Capets'. Idea 3 (a nation may govern itself, but hereditary government is for people not yet existing or minors, so the right does not exist and assuming it is treason against posterity): d07-p045, 'government by hereditary succession is government for another race of people, and not for itself; and as those on whom it is to operate are not yet in existence, or are minors ... to assume such a right is treason against the right of posterity'.

Idea 1 (origin: man himself, by right of his existence): d07-p048, 'Its origin is ever in view. Man is himself the origin and the evidence of the right. It appertains to him in right of his existence'. Idea 2 (basis: equality of rights, one vote each, neither rich nor poor may exclude the other; exclusion is force not right): d07-p049, 'The true and only true basis of representative government is equality of Rights. Every man has a right to one vote, and no more', 'The rich have no more right to exclude the poor ... than the poor have to exclude the rich ... it is a question of force and not of right'.

Idea 1 (a combination of those with the property to exclude those without, a self-created part of society): d07-p051, 'it is a combination of the persons possessing that quantity to exclude those who do not possess the same quantity. It is investing themselves with powers as a self-created part of society'. Idea 2 (arbitrary power and robbery; voting is property of the most sacred kind): d07-p050, 'not only to assume arbitrary power, but to assume a right to commit robbery. Personal rights, of which the right of voting for representatives is one, are a species of property of the most sacred kind'. Idea 3 (opposers never mean the exclusion for themselves; this has been fatal to thousands who sought more and lost all): d07-p052, 'those who oppose an equality of rights never mean the exclusion should take place on themselves', 'This opinion has already been fatal to thousands, who, not contented with equal rights, have sought more till they lost all'.

Idea 1 (a considerable sum excludes the majority, unites them against the government, which they can overturn): d07-p053, 'it will exclude a majority of the people, and unite them in a common interest against the government ... they can overturn such a government and its supporters whenever they please'. Idea 2 (a small sum disgraces liberty by tying it to accident; mare and mule): d07-p054, 'it exhibits liberty in disgrace, by putting it in competition with accident and insignificance. When a broodmare shall fortunately produce a foal or a mule that ... shall convey to its owner the right of voting, or by its death take it from him'. Idea 3 (property acquired without merit, lost without crime): d07-p054, 'how many ways property may be acquired without merit, and lost without a crime'.

Idea 1 (the right by which other rights are protected; without a vote a man is subject to another's will, which is slavery; disfranchising as criminal as taking property): d07-p056, 'the primary right by which other rights are protected. To take away this right is to reduce a man to slavery, for slavery consists in being subject to the will of another', 'as criminal as the proposal to take away property'. Idea 2 (government's strength is in proportion to the number interested in supporting it; exclusion from voting cannot exclude rebellion): d07-p057, 'the strength and permanent security of government is in proportion to the number of people interested in supporting it', 'it is impossible to exclude them from the right of rebelling against that exclusion'.

Idea 1 (in a company rights come only from property invested): d07-p060, 'the rights of the members composing that company are wholly created by the property they invest therein'. Idea 2 (civil government has cognizance of every man, so every kind of right must be represented; person more sacred than property; the faculty of work is property): d07-p061, 'has cognizance of everything, and of every man ... whether he has property or not ... every kind of right, be represented', 'The protection of a man's person is more sacred than the protection of property', 'the faculty of performing any kind of work ... is of the nature of property'. Idea 3 (equal rights remove complaint and violence, so property is secure; property as a pretence for unequal rights provokes indignation and tumult): d07-p062, 'to remove ... every cause of complaint, and every motive to violence; and this can only be done by an equality of rights. Idea 1 (rights are not gifts, for none could be the first giver; they belong to man by his existence and so are equal): d07-p070, 'rights are not gifts from one man to another, nor from one class of men to another; for who is he who could be the first giver', 'rights appertain to man in right of his existence only, and must therefore be equal to every man'. Idea 1 (equal rights are principle; the arrangement of the parts of government is opinion): d07-p073, 'Whether the rights of men shall be equal is not a matter of opinion but of right, and consequently of principle', 'the manner in which the several parts of government shall be arranged and composed, it is altogether matter of opinion'. Idea 1 (the worst is the legislature crowded into one body, subject to the precipitancy and passion of an individual): d07-p076, 'That is the worst, which in its deliberations and decisions is subject to the precipitancy and passion of an individual; and when the whole legislature is crowded into one body it is an individual in mass'. Idea 4 (avidity to punish is dangerous; guard even an enemy from oppression): d07-p086, 'An avidity to punish is always dangerous to liberty', 'must guard even his enemy from oppression'.

Idea 1 (as with the limit of a man's life, known by observation, a system showing symptoms of decay will dissolve and the period can be calculated): d08-p003, 'we can always fix a period beyond which man cannot live ... by observation of what has happened in all cases', 'exhibits in its progress a series of symptoms indicating decay, its final dissolution is certain, and the period of it can be calculated from the symptoms'. Idea 1 (each term is the preceding one plus its half, a fast-growing series): d08-p020, 'in the series of one half upon each preceding number; like the numbers 8, 12, 18, 27'; d08-p021, 'how rapidly the sums increase as the ratio proceeds'. Idea 1 (prices are in proportion to the quantity of money; with gold and silver only, prices were nearly stationary): d08-p038, 'the price of labour, or of the produce of labour ... will be in proportion to the quantity of money in a country', 'nature gives out those metals with a sparing hand ... so nearly stationary as to vary but little'. Idea 1 (the twenty-one million war was a victorious confederacy of England, Austria and Holland): d08-p040, 'The war that cost twenty-one millions was the war of the confederates ... Idea 1 (paper pulled gold and silver down to its level; coin buys less than without paper or where there is none): d08-p041, 'the paper has pulled down the value of gold and silver to a level with itself. Idea 1 (taxes and interest are paid in bank notes; too little gold and silver to pay the taxes in coin): d08-p048, 'taxes in England are not paid in gold and silver, but in paper (bank notes)', 'There is not gold and silver enough in the nation to pay the taxes in coin', 'The interest of the national funded debt is paid at the bank in the same kind of paper'. Idea 2 (the coin is spread through the country and in tills, so the bank holds under two millions, probably one): d08-p050, 'every city, town, village, and farmhouse in the nation must have a part of it', 'a few guineas in his till', 'can never ... be so much as two millions; most probably not more than one million'. Idea 3 (on this slender twig hangs the system of four hundred millions and many millions of notes): d08-p050, 'on this slender twig ... hangs the whole funding system of four hundred millions, besides many millions in bank notes'.
